system.name: WR 104
system.description: A Wolf-Rayet binary system 5,200 light-years away in Sagittarius, famous for its perfect pinwheel nebula. The system's orbital plane may point almost directly at Earth, raising speculation about gamma-ray burst exposure — though most researchers consider the risk negligible.

wr104.name: WR 104 (Ve 2-45)
wr104.description: A WC9d Wolf-Rayet star — the exposed carbon-oxygen core of a massive star that has shed its outer layers through intense stellar winds. Its interaction with the OB companion creates a spiral dust plume as the two winds collide and cool, producing a spectacular rotating pinwheel nebula.
wr104.funFact: WR 104's dust pinwheel is so geometrically perfect that it was used to determine the orbital period with millimetre-precision interferometry — measuring a rotating spiral 200 AU across from 5,200 light-years away.

wr104b.name: WR 104 B
wr104b.description: A massive OB companion of roughly 25 solar masses whose powerful stellar wind collides with that of the Wolf-Rayet primary, compressing material into a spiral dust plume that rotates once every 241.5 days. Its greater mass means the barycenter sits closer to it than to the WR star.
wr104b.funFact: The WR 104 pinwheel was one of the first stellar wind-collision spirals ever imaged directly — the Keck telescope resolved it as a spinning dust corkscrew that expands at roughly 1,000 km/s.
